content: Airsickness is a condition triggered by air travel and is a specific type of motion sickness. It is considered a normal physiological response in healthy individuals. The condition arises when the central nervous system receives conflicting sensory inputs from the body, particularly from the inner ear, eyes, and muscles, which disrupt balance and equilibrium. The inner ear plays a critical role in maintaining balance as it contains sensors for both angular (rotational) and linear motion. Airsickness typically manifests as a combination of spatial disorientation, nausea, and vomiting. Experimental studies have shown that removing the nodulus of the vermis, a part of the cerebellum, can eliminate airsickness in monkeys. Common symptoms of airsickness include nausea, vomiting, vertigo, loss of appetite, cold sweating, pale skin, difficulty concentrating, confusion, drowsiness, headache, and increased fatigue. In severe cases, airsickness can incapacitate an individual entirely. Certain factors increase susceptibility to airsickness. Fatigue, stress, and anxiety are known to heighten the likelihood of motion sickness in general. The use of alcohol, drugs, or medications can also contribute to the development of airsickness. Women, particularly during menstruation or pregnancy, young children, and individuals prone to other forms of motion sickness are more likely to experience airsickness. While experienced pilots rarely suffer from airsickness, it is more common among student pilots. To minimize symptoms, travelers prone to motion sickness can take several precautions. Choosing seats with the smoothest ride, such as those over the wings of an airplane, can help. Sitting facing forward and focusing on distant objects, rather than reading or looking at items inside the airplane, is also beneficial. Consuming dry crackers, olives, or sucking on a lemon can help dry out the mouth and reduce nausea. Drinking carbonated beverages may also provide relief. Medications that may alleviate airsickness symptoms include meclizine (Antivert, Bonine), dimenhydrinate (Dramamine), diphenhydramine (Benadryl), and scopolamine (available in both patch and oral forms). Ginger capsules are another option. However, pilots should avoid anti-motion sickness medications, whether prescription or over-the-counter, as these drugs can cause drowsiness or impair cognitive function. Non-pharmacologic remedies include repeated exposure to the flight environment that initially caused airsickness. This method, known as habituation, can reduce an individual’s susceptibility to subsequent episodes of airsickness. Additionally, devices designed to reduce motion sickness by stimulating specific body parts, such as the wrist, have been introduced. These products, marketed under names like Sea Bands and Relief Band, lack clinical evidence supporting their effectiveness. Natural remedies for motion sickness are also widely used. Ginger derivatives, such as ginger tea or powdered ginger capsules, are among the most popular. In tests conducted by the hosts of the American television program Mythbusters, ginger was found to be one of the most effective non-prescription remedies for motion sickness.
